lines.text: Four and a half billion years, from a molten young planet to the first cells, the dinosaurs and us. This is the long story of life on Earth.
It begins with a collision. A planet about the size of Mars, called Theia, is thought to have struck the young Earth and been almost wholly destroyed.
This first eon, the Hadean, was a hot and violent time, the surface pounded by impacts, though the first oceans may already have gathered.
Out of it came our Earth, about four and a half billion years ago: the third planet from the Sun, and the only place we know of with life.
The debris of that crash came together as the Moon. Ever since, it has raised the tides and kept the Earth's tilt steady.
Then, some four billion years ago, the inner planets may have taken a storm of asteroids and comets, recorded in the rocks brought back from the Moon.
In the Archean the first continents grew, and in the sea the oldest known life appeared: simple single cells, in air with almost no oxygen.
The Proterozoic was the longest eon of all, nearly two billion years, in which oxygen built up, complex cells arose and supercontinents came and went.
Microbes that fed on sunlight made oxygen, and around two and a half billion years ago it began to fill the air, rusting the seas and poisoning older life.
Over a billion and a half years ago came a new kind of cell, one that kept its DNA in a nucleus. Every plant, animal and fungus descends from it.
Then the planet froze. Ice may have reached the tropics and covered almost everything, until volcanoes breathed out enough carbon dioxide to warm it again.
The first faint signs of animals date from about six hundred and sixty million years ago: many-celled creatures that eat other living things.
In the Ediacaran, the first large complex life spread across the sea floor, soft creatures shaped like fronds and discs, unlike anything alive today.
About five hundred and forty million years ago the Paleozoic opened, the era of ancient life that would bring fish, forests and the first animals on land.
It began with a burst. In the Cambrian explosion most of the great animal groups appear in the rocks within a few tens of millions of years.
Among them were the arthropods, with jointed legs and armour on the outside. Insects, spiders and crabs belong to this, the largest group of animals.
Fish came soon after, the first animals with a backbone. Every later vertebrate, ourselves included, comes from this line.
By about four hundred and sixty million years ago fungi were clearly there too, breaking down dead matter in a kingdom all their own.
Then the first of the five great extinctions struck. Ice lowered the seas, warming followed, and most species in the oceans were lost.
Life recovered in the Devonian, the age of fishes. Sharks and armoured fish ruled the water, the first forests grew, and some fish grew limbs.
On land, the relatives of insects appear around four hundred million years ago, the start of the most varied animals on Earth.
Late in the Devonian a run of extinctions hit the shallow seas hard, wiping out reef builders and armoured fish, perhaps as the water lost its oxygen.
In the Carboniferous, swampy forests laid down the coal we burn today, and in air rich with oxygen, giant insects took to the wing.
Meanwhile the continents drifted together into one great landmass, Pangaea, ringed by a single vast ocean.
Frogs and salamanders trace their line to around this time, animals that live part of their lives in water and part on land.
Two hundred and fifty million years ago the Mesozoic began, the age of reptiles, when dinosaurs would rule the land and sea reptiles the oceans.
Its first period, the Triassic, was a time of rebuilding. The first dinosaurs, flying pterosaurs and small mammals appeared.
That rebuilding followed the Great Dying, the worst extinction ever, when vast eruptions in Siberia heated the world and most life in the sea perished.
In the new seas swam ichthyosaurs, dolphin-shaped reptiles that breathed air. Mary Anning's finds in England later helped prove such animals had vanished.
The Jurassic followed, named after the Jura Mountains: the time of giant long-necked dinosaurs, the first birds, and an Atlantic beginning to open.
Its door was opened by another extinction, as Pangaea split and great eruptions changed the climate, clearing the way for the dinosaurs.
In the oceans, plesiosaurs paddled on four flippers, many with very long necks, the animals the Loch Ness legend is so often compared to.
As the continents tore apart, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge began making new sea floor, a hidden mountain chain that later helped prove plate tectonics.
And quietly, in the shadow of the dinosaurs, came the mammals: small, warm-blooded and furry, feeding their young on milk.
In the late Jurassic of what is now the American West walked Stegosaurus, with tall plates down its back, spikes on its tail and a tiny brain.
It had good reason for the spikes. Allosaurus, the top hunter of its day, stalked on two legs with a big head and curved teeth.
Diplodocus was one of the longest animals ever, with a slender neck and a whip of a tail. Casts of its skeleton now stand in museums worldwide.
Brachiosaurus stood like a giraffe, its front legs longer than its back, reaching the tops of trees no one else could.
In Germany lived Archaeopteryx, with feathers and wings but also teeth and a bony tail. Found in 1861, it linked birds to dinosaurs.
Above it flew Pterodactylus, a small reptile on wings of skin, and the first pterosaur ever to be given a name.
The Cretaceous was the last chapter of the dinosaurs, with warm, high seas and flowers spreading across the land.
Those flowering plants changed everything. Today they are the largest group on land, and almost every crop we grow is one of them.
In North Africa, Spinosaurus hunted fish in the rivers, a giant with a sail on its back and a snout like a crocodile's.
In Europe grazed Iguanodon, a plant eater with a spike on each thumb, and only the second dinosaur science ever named.
Deinonychus was fast and feathered, with a great claw on each foot. Its study in the sixties showed dinosaurs as active, bird-like animals.
And in South America lived Argentinosaurus, among the heaviest land animals there have ever been, though we know it from only a few bones.
Mosasaurus ruled the late Cretaceous seas, a huge relative of lizards. A skull found near Maastricht helped convince scientists that species can die out.
Velociraptor was far smaller than the film version, a feathered hunter about the size of a turkey, from the deserts of Mongolia.
By about seventy-two million years ago modern birds had appeared, the one branch of the dinosaurs that would survive what was coming.
Now came the most famous of them all, Tyrannosaurus rex, with a huge skull and one of the strongest bites of any land animal.
It shared its land with Triceratops, a plant eater with a bony frill and three horns, one of the very last dinosaurs.
Ankylosaurus was built like a tank, covered in bony armour and swinging a heavy club of bone at the end of its tail.
Overhead soared Quetzalcoatlus, a pterosaur with wings about as wide as a small aeroplane, one of the largest flyers of all time.
Sixty-six million years ago a new era began, the Cenozoic, the age of mammals, which runs right up to today.
It opened with catastrophe. An asteroid perhaps ten kilometres wide hit what is now Mexico, leaving a crater nearly two hundred kilometres across.
Dust darkened the skies, and about three quarters of all species died, among them every dinosaur except the birds.
With the reptiles gone, the world kept changing. India crashed into Asia and pushed up the Himalayas, which are rising still.
Some lines that began in this era have ended only lately, like the baiji, a pale dolphin of the Yangtze, found nowhere in a survey in 2006.
In New Zealand evolved the moa, flightless birds well over two metres tall, gone within a couple of centuries of the first people arriving.
Madagascar had its elephant birds, among the heaviest birds ever, laying the largest eggs known, until people settled the island.
And on Mauritius lived the dodo. Sailors arrived in the late fifteen hundreds, and within a century it was gone, a symbol of extinction ever since.
Back in Africa, about seven million years ago, lived Sahelanthropus, known from one skull in Chad, perhaps among the first of the human line.
Ardipithecus, from Ethiopia, could walk upright on the ground and still climb in the trees of its woodland home.
In North America the passenger pigeon once flew in flocks of millions. Hunting and felled forests ended it, and the last one, Martha, died in a zoo.
South America had a ground sloth as big as an elephant, rearing on its hind legs to pull down leaves, until soon after people came.
In East Africa, Australopithecus afarensis walked on two legs with long arms and a small brain, an early cousin of ours.
At Laetoli in Tanzania, its kind left footprints in volcanic ash, among the oldest direct proof of walking upright.
Over three million years ago the Stone Age began, the long age of stone tools that lasted until people learned to work metal.
Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974, is about forty percent of one skeleton, and showed our ancestors walked upright long before their brains grew large.
The oldest tools we know are Oldowan: pebbles struck to give sharp edges, for cutting meat and scraping hides, made for about a million years.
Then came the Pleistocene, the great age of ice, of mammoths and sabre-toothed cats, in which our own kind would evolve and spread.
Its ice age has never quite ended. Ice sheets have grown and shrunk again and again, and we live in a warm gap between them.
In the Americas hunted Smilodon, the best known sabre-toothed cat, whose bones fill the tar pits of La Brea by the thousand.
Glyptodon, a cousin of the armadillo the size of a small car, carried a dome of bony plates and was hunted by early people.
In East Africa, Paranthropus boisei chewed tough plants with huge jaws and flat teeth, living beside early Homo but leaving no descendants.
Homo habilis, the handy man, is one of the first of our own genus, found beside stone tools in East Africa.
In Australia the thylacine arose, a striped pouched hunter called the Tasmanian tiger. The last known one died in a Hobart zoo in 1936.
The aurochs, a huge wild ox painted on cave walls, gave us our farm cattle. The last of them died in a Polish forest in the sixteen twenties.
Homo erectus had a body much like ours. It walked far, used fire and spread out of Africa across Asia, and lasted well over a million years.
Its tool was the hand axe, a carefully shaped teardrop of stone, made across three continents for more than a million years.
About a million years ago come the first signs that humans kept fire, for warmth, for safety and for cooking: one of the biggest steps of all.
Homo heidelbergensis, in Africa and Europe, made fine tools and spears, and may be the common ancestor of Neanderthals and of us.
Neanderthals lived through the ice age in Europe and western Asia. They made tools, kept fire and buried their dead, and many of us carry their DNA.
Woolly mammoths roamed the cold plains of three continents. People hunted them, and a last small group lived on an Arctic island until about four thousand years ago.
The Denisovans, a human group identified only in 2010 from DNA and a few bones, also left their genes in some living people.
The Irish elk was a giant deer with antlers some three metres across, and despite its name, it was neither only Irish nor a true elk.
On the steppes of Eurasia the woolly rhinoceros grazed in thick fur, painted in caves and sometimes found frozen whole.
Deep in a South African cave lay Homo naledi, small-brained and yet alive at the same time as early modern humans.
And about three hundred thousand years ago, in Africa, our own species was taking shape. Homo sapiens would reach every continent.
In Europe, cave bears slept through the winters in the same caves that people sometimes used, eating mostly plants.
In South Africa the quagga appeared, a zebra striped only at the front. Settlers hunted it out, and the last died in Amsterdam's zoo.
On the island of Flores lived the hobbit, Homo floresiensis, about a metre tall, until people like us arrived.
In ice age America the dire wolf, heavier than any wolf today, hunted the great beasts, and it too ended up in the tar pits of La Brea.
Then, at the end of the ice age, most of the largest land mammals vanished. A changing climate and human hunters both share the blame.
While the seas were low, Beringia joined Siberia to Alaska, a grassy plain on which animals and people crossed into the Americas.
In the caves of Lascaux in France, people painted horses, stags and bulls about seventeen thousand years ago. The art was rediscovered in 1940.
With them began the sixth extinction, still going on, in which species vanish far faster than normal, mostly because of us.
About twelve thousand years ago the ice drew back and the Holocene began, a warm, steady time in which farming, cities and all of history unfolded.
In the seventeen hundreds Carl Linnaeus gave every living thing a two-part Latin name, like Homo sapiens. Biologists still sort life his way.
In 1741 explorers found Steller's sea cow, a gentle kelp grazer eight metres long. Within about thirty years it had been hunted to the last.
The great auk, a flightless seabird like a big penguin, went the same way. The last known pair were killed off Iceland in 1844.
America's only native parrot, the bright Carolina parakeet, was shot by farmers, and the last known one died in the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918.
Then came the man who explained it all. Charles Darwin sailed on the Beagle and spent decades working out evolution by natural selection.
In a monastery garden in Moravia, the friar Gregor Mendel bred thousands of pea plants and found that traits pass on in fixed patterns.
Working in Southeast Asia, Alfred Russel Wallace reached the same idea as Darwin on his own, and his letter in 1858 pushed Darwin to publish.
The Pyrenean ibex, a wild goat of Spain and France, lost its last female in 2000. A clone born three years later lived only minutes.
In 1859 Darwin published On the Origin of Species, and changed for good how people see living things and their own place among them.
Mendel's rules of heredity appeared in 1866 but were ignored for over thirty years. Rediscovered around 1900, they founded genetics.
Lonesome George was the last Pinta Island tortoise. Scientists searched for a mate for him in vain, and when he died in 2012 his kind ended.
From 1960 Jane Goodall watched wild chimpanzees at Gombe and saw them make and use tools, then spent her life fighting to protect wild places.
The western black rhino of West Africa was not so lucky. Poachers drove it down, and in 2011 it was declared extinct.
Some call our time the Anthropocene, an age in which people reshape the climate, oceans and species, though geologists voted in 2024 not to make it official.
In 1953 Watson and Crick, building on the X-ray images of Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, found DNA's double helix, and how life copies itself.
The golden toad of a Costa Rican cloud forest was last seen in 1989, among the first species lost to climate change and disease.
And in the sixties plate tectonics was accepted at last: the slow drift of the plates that built the mountains and carried life's stage around the world.
From one cell in an ancient sea to a species that can read its own code, life's story is still being written.
